source.title: UnrealNAS: Can We Search Neural Architectures with Unreal Data?
source.authors: Zhen Dong; Kai-Chen Zhou; G. Li; Qiang Zhou; Ming-Fei Guo; Bernard Ghanem; K. Keutzer; Shang-Hang Zhang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses randomly labeled or unreal data to search for architectures, then reports how those architectures perform after retraining on natural-label tasks. It does not test whether the same networks that fit random labels also generalize when trained on natural labels.
record.gate_note: The random-label probe-net convergence and architecture-ranking results concern dataset difficulty and architecture selection, not the training-to-test gap in the claim. The downstream test-error results are recorded under fits_no_version because none of the listed versions covers architecture search on unreal data followed by natural-label retraining.
record.test_reason: UnrealNAS uses random-label learning to select architectures and reports their performance after natural-label retraining. Section 3.1 measures convergence and architecture-ranking correlations, but does not establish V1's paired random-label memorization and natural-label generalization result under the same architecture and training recipe. No experiment tests V2–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that unreal search data and random labels can select architectures with competitive downstream performance, and argue that difficult proxy tasks help distinguish effective capacity. The absence of real data or labels applies to architecture search; downstream training uses natural-label datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper searches architectures with random labels or generated data, then retrains selected architectures on natural-label downstream datasets. It does not compare the generalization gap of a fixed network trained on natural versus random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of random-label classes affects search performance; when data per class is sufficient, more classes can help, while too many classes for random noise can hurt and destabilize search. Search data type also changes the reported downstream results.

fits_no_version.finding: Architectures selected using random-label real images, fractal images, or Gaussian noise achieve competitive downstream performance after natural-label retraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Differentiable architecture search can use unreal proxy tasks to select effective architectures for natural-label image tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.1 reports convergence scores of 31, 71, 36, and 94 for natural CIFAR-10, randomly labeled CIFAR-10, fractal images, and Gaussian noise. Unreal-task training-accuracy rankings correlate with CIFAR-100 test-accuracy rankings: Kendall tau is 0.64, 0.60, and 0.58.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning performance on difficult unreal tasks can help rank architectures by downstream natural-label performance.

record.problems: The reported downstream test errors and accuracies do not include corresponding training errors, so they cannot establish a training-to-test gap. Some comparisons are against results from other papers, as the text states.
record.rows_left_out: The probe-net convergence scores and Kendall Tau architecture-ranking correlations in Section 3.1 were left out because they measure dataset difficulty and architecture ranking, not the generalization gap in the claim. Figure-only class-count ablation values in Figure 6 were also left out.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting and above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy for the same architecture and recipe, together with chance held-out performance after random-label training.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning. Using Adam for architecture parameters and SGD for network weights is not such a comparison.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record overemphasizes missing training-to-test gaps: several versions concern held-out performance directly. The decisive issue here is the absence of the specific comparisons each version requires. Search and retraining also differ in network size and training duration; Appendix 7 specifies different weight decay and data pipelines for real and unreal search tasks. Unreal-task validation uses transformed training examples, so its accuracy is not independent held-out random-label generalization. The omitted probe and ranking results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the same network and training recipe fitting random labels and then generalizing when trained on natural labels; does not report held-out accuracy for networks trained on random labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD for generalization.
No comparison of batch sizes or large-batch generalization gaps.
No sharpness or other measured property is related to a training-to-test gap.
